Plato. Four hundred and twenty-eight to three hundred and forty-eight BCE. He was an Athenian philosopher and student of Socrates who founded the Academy and authored the dialogues that preserve Socrates' method while advancing his own metaphysics, epistemology, and ethics. His theory of eternal, immaterial forms shaped Western thought for two millennia. His Republic remains the foundational text of political philosophy.

Plato was born into a wealthy Athenian family and became Socrates' student around age twenty. He witnessed Socrates' trial and execution, an event that haunted him and drove much of his philosophy. He founded the Academy in Athens around three hundred and eighty-seven BCE, an institution for philosophical inquiry and mathematics that lasted nearly nine hundred years. He authored approximately thirty surviving dialogues, almost all featuring Socrates as the main speaker.

The theory of forms is central to his thought. He posited a realm of eternal, immutable, abstract forms or ideas transcending the physical world. Physical objects are imperfect copies or shadows of the forms. A physical chair participates in the form of Chair. Forms explain universals and permanence. The material world is flux and illusion. Only through reason and philosophical contemplation can we grasp forms. Sensory experience is unreliable.

In the Republic, Plato sketched an ideal state where philosopher-kings rule. These rulers are educated in mathematics and dialectic. Virtue arises from knowledge and the harmony of the soul's three parts: reason, spirit, and appetite. Justice is the right ordering of these parts. The just state mirrors the just soul. He rejected democracy, which he witnessed fail in Athens. He advocated rule by the wise and educated.

His method is the Platonic dialogue. Socrates engages an interlocutor, exposes their confusion, and points toward truth through questioning. He influenced Aristotle, his student, as well as medieval theology through Augustine and Aquinas, Renaissance philosophy, and modern metaphysics through Descartes and Kant. Plato stands at the crossroads of Western intellectual history. His theory of transcendent forms answered the pre-Socratic puzzle of permanence and change. It shaped every metaphysical tradition that appeals to abstract universals or eternal truths. The Academy was the first research university. His dialogues are literature and philosophy simultaneously, making Socrates immortal through dialogue. Platonism—the belief in a realm beyond the material—recurs in theology, mathematics, and logic across two thousand years.
